chapterBreakdown.gentle: A persuasive setup can work before anyone asks whether it should have been used. Chapter 13 moves to that earlier checkpoint. It says the first pre-suasive decision is ethical: whether the approach deserves use at all. The frozen support also warns that commercial communicators often place profit above ethics. That matters because success can start to look like its own excuse. The chapter resists that shortcut. It argues that unethical tactics may damage organizational profits even when they seem useful in the moment. The practical lesson is simple. An effective setup is not automatically a legitimate one.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Some influence moves succeed because they are skillful, but Chapter 13 asks whether they are fair enough to use. It shifts the book to the earlier ethical gate that comes before tactic design. The support says profit often outranks ethics in commercial settings, which makes effectiveness feel like the only test. The chapter rejects that standard. It argues that unethical tactics can backfire against the organization itself, even while they appear to help in the short run. The point is not to deny effectiveness. It is to separate what works from what deserves to be used.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: A sharp setup can win the moment and still lose the case for using it. Chapter 13 moves the fight upstream. Before choosing a cue, the real call is whether the move clears an ethical gate. The support warns that profit-first thinking invites misuse, because a tactic that converts can start looking self-justifying. The chapter cuts against that logic. Unethical influence may score now while undercutting organizational gain later. The hard rule here is plain. A move that works is not automatically a move you earned the right to run.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A persuasive setup can look impressive while still raising the wrong question too late. Chapter 13 moves that question earlier. Instead of asking only which cue, frame, or arrangement will increase receptivity, it asks whether the pre-suasive approach deserves use on ethical grounds in the first place. That is why the chapter calls the issue a pre-pre-suasive consideration: the moral checkpoint comes before tactic design.

The frozen support keeps the argument narrow. Commercial communicators often place profit above ethics. That pressure matters because a tactic that works can begin to feel self-justifying. If the audience becomes more compliant, the method can start to look acceptable simply because it delivered a result. Chapter 13 resists that shortcut by separating effectiveness from legitimacy.

The support also gives the chapter a practical edge. It argues against unethical use by citing studies indicating that such tactics undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The frozen bundle does not list those ways, so the chapter should not pretend to know them. Still, the direction is clear enough: a method that exploits people can damage the very outcomes it was supposed to improve.

That makes this chapter a gate inside the book's optimization section. It does not abandon pre-suasion. It asks what kinds of pre-suasion should never be engineered. The lesson is that a useful move still has to earn its right to be used.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
An influence move can succeed technically while failing the earlier test Chapter 13 cares about. This chapter shifts attention from design skill to ethical permission. Before choosing the setup, the pre-suader has to decide whether the approach should be employed at all.

The support keeps the frame focused. In commercial settings, profit is often allowed to outrank ethics. Once that happens, effectiveness can masquerade as justification. A tactic that lifts response rates may start to feel legitimate merely because it wins. Chapter 13 breaks that equation. The first question is not whether the move can work. It is whether the move deserves use.

The chapter also makes that case in practical terms. It says unethical tactics can undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The details are not spelled out in the frozen support, so the chapter must stay disciplined there. Yet the claim is enough to show the pattern: a profit-first shortcut can injure the very organization it tries to help.

That is the chapter's real contribution. It turns ethics into an earlier gate rather than a later apology. Skill matters, but legitimacy comes first.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A persuasive edge is not clean just because it converts. Chapter 13 moves the test upstream and asks whether the move should even be in play. The chapter's title signals that ethics comes before setup design, not after the numbers come in.

The frozen support names the pressure point. Commercial communicators often put profit above ethics. When that happens, success starts laundering the method. If the tactic lands, people can treat performance as proof that the move was acceptable. Chapter 13 refuses that deal by splitting tactical force from moral clearance.

It also refuses the false comfort that profit-first influence is at least good business. The chapter says unethical tactics can undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The source does not authorize the list, so the chapter must stay narrow. But it clearly authorizes the warning: a move can juice the moment and still make the organization pay later.

That is why this chapter matters inside the optimization section. It does not merely ask how to sharpen influence. It asks which sharpened moves should never leave the box.

chapterBreakdown.gentle:
A communicator can know exactly how to prepare a room and still be answering the wrong question first. Chapter 13 identifies that error by moving the ethical issue ahead of design. After a long run of chapters about readiness, attention, association, and unity, the book pauses to ask whether a pre-suasive approach should be employed on ethical grounds before any cue or arrangement is selected. The chapter's title, Ethical Use: A Pre-Pre-Suasive Consideration, marks that relocation clearly.

The frozen support keeps the argument focused rather than expansive. It does not offer a full business-ethics system, and it does not authorize a broad legal lecture. Instead, it names one recurring pressure: commercial communicators often place profit above ethics. That pressure matters because success can disguise itself as innocence. If a setup improves response, the method can start to feel vindicated by its own performance. Chapter 13 breaks that reflex. A result is not the same thing as a right.

This matters because pre-suasion works before the audience has fully evaluated the later request. It shapes conditions, salience, and receptivity in advance. That power can be used to clarify, to prepare honest attention, and to improve the fit between message and audience. It can also be used to exploit a moment, obscure the real basis of agreement, or borrow cooperation a proposal has not earned. The chapter therefore asks the earliest question available: should this move be run at all?

The support also gives the chapter a practical anti-cynicism argument. It says unethical tactics undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The frozen source does not license the specifics, so the chapter has to stay narrower than curiosity would prefer. But the stated direction is still revealing. Profit-first misuse is not simply morally suspect while economically clever. It can be self-defeating on the organization's own terms. The shortcut can injure the very interests used to defend it.

That is what makes Chapter 13 more than a moral footnote. It reframes optimization itself. The task is not merely to find the strongest lever. The task is to decide which levers deserve use, even when they promise lift. A pre-suader who treats ethics as a later clean-up step has already missed the chapter's point, because the crucial decision was supposed to happen before the mechanism was built.

The chapter therefore keeps one distinction under pressure from beginning to end. Tactical effectiveness and ethical legitimacy are related, but they are not interchangeable. A move can win now and still fail the deeper test. It can even appear profit-smart while quietly taxing trust, standing, or future cooperation in ways the frozen source summarizes without enumerating. Chapter 13's discipline is to stop that slippage early and insist that permission comes before engineering.

From there the book can close on its final issue. Once a move has cleared the ethical gate and succeeded honestly, a new question appears: will the change last? Chapter 13 sets up that turn by reminding the reader that influence is accountable both before the moment and after it.
chapterBreakdown.direct:
A pre-suader can master setup design and still fail the chapter that asks the more basic question. Chapter 13 moves the decision point upstream. Before selecting the cue, frame, or arrangement, the communicator has to decide whether the approach deserves use on ethical grounds at all. That is the force of calling the issue a pre-pre-suasive consideration.

The support keeps the chapter disciplined. It does not authorize a broad doctrine of business morality. It names a narrower pressure: commercial communicators often put profit above ethics. Once that happens, a tactic that performs well can begin to look justified by output alone. Chapter 13 rejects that move. Performance is evidence of force, not proof of legitimacy.

That distinction matters because pre-suasion alters the field before the request is judged. It can direct attention honestly, prepare relevance, and help a message land under fair conditions. It can also exploit a vulnerable opening or build leverage the later proposal has not earned. The chapter therefore asks the earliest operational question available: should this tactic be used at all, not merely can it work?

The practical warning sharpens the point. The support says unethical tactics undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The source stops there, so the chapter must stop there too. But that narrow claim is enough to overturn a lazy assumption. Profit-first misuse is not just ethically weak while commercially smart. It can be strategically self-defeating.

That is why Chapter 13 changes the meaning of optimization. Better persuasion is not only about stronger engineering. It is about refusing to engineer moves that fail the legitimacy test. When ethics is treated as a later review step, the real decision has already been made too late.

The chapter keeps one hard distinction intact. A tactic can succeed in the short run and still be wrong to use. It can even seem like a profitable shortcut while quietly working against the organization's longer game. Chapter 13 forces the reader to separate skill from permission before moving into the book's final concern about durability.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
A move can be lethal in the room and still be illegitimate before it starts. Chapter 13 pushes the judgment point upstream and refuses to let design skill answer the ethical question by force. The title says what the chapter is doing: the real checkpoint comes before setup design, not after a tactic posts a win.

The frozen support names the pressure that makes this hard. Commercial communicators often rank profit above ethics. Once that ranking takes hold, performance begins scrubbing the method. If the move converts, people start acting like the numbers cleared it. Chapter 13 breaks that laundering cycle by separating a move's power from its right to run.

That split matters because pre-suasion shapes the field before the audience has fully judged the ask. Used well, that power can prepare honest attention. Used badly, it can exploit a moment the proposal did not earn. The chapter therefore asks the first serious question, not the second one. Do you have the right to use this move at all?

The chapter also kills the fantasy that profit-first misuse is at least smart business. The support says unethical tactics undermine organizational profits in three potent ways. The source does not license the list, so the prose has to stay tight. But it clearly licenses the verdict: a dirty edge can charge the moment while taxing your own side later.

That makes Chapter 13 more than a sermon bolted onto a tactics book. It changes the standard for what counts as optimization. Sharpening influence is not enough. You also have to reject sharpened moves that fail the legitimacy gate. If ethics shows up only after deployment, the real call was already blown.

The chapter holds one line all the way through. A move that works is not automatically a move you earned the right to use. Short-run gains can mask long-run costs, including costs the source summarizes without itemizing. Chapter 13 forces the audit before the build, then hands the book to its final question: once a clean move succeeds, what makes the change stick?
